A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same weight-based tracing and reversal research. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on identifying ROME edits, predicting relations, extracting edited objects and reversing edits, including CounterFact and Yago results.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds experiments across editing methods, downstream tasks, and batch and sequential editing scenarios.

M1.justification: v2 Appendix E adapts reversal from intervention on one edited matrix to simultaneous bottom-rank approximation of all matrices affected by multi-layer editors. The fixed-token, cross-entropy tracing procedure and SVD truncation remain fundamentally unchanged; naming the tracing procedure EditScope does not itself introduce a new method.

E1.justification: CounterFact, Yago and wikitext-103 are retained; Yago was already present in v1's appendix. v2 adds downstream evaluation on CoLA, MMLU, MRPC, NLI, RTE and SST, and extends reversal from isolated edits to batch and sequential editing scenarios in Appendices F–G.

E2.justification: The random relation-prediction baseline and k=0/no-reversal control are retained. The added r-ROME, MEMIT, MEND and AlphaEdit methods generate the edits being examined; they are not competing tracing or reversal methods evaluated against the proposed countermeasures.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce Qwen2.5-7B and Mistral-7B configurations, training the layer preceding multi-layer edits, KL-divergence and downstream F1 measurements, and much larger truncation sweeps. Batch experiments edit 1,000 facts, while sequential experiments use 1,000 facts in batches of 100. The original tracing splits and optimizer settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 Section 5.3 adds analyses asking whether reversal restores the output distribution and preserves downstream capabilities. Appendices E–G test generalization and failure conditions across editing mechanisms and batch/sequential settings. The original layer/rank sensitivity, weight-pattern and unique-prediction analyses remain present.

E5.justification: v2 first reports five-seed means and standard deviations for ROME/r-ROME object tracing and three-seed estimates for the additional editors. Conversely, it removes standard deviations from the retained CounterFact relation-prediction and CounterFact/Yago reversal tables. These additions and removals substantially change uncertainty reporting for central results.

E6.justification: The original three-model ROME reversal means are unchanged in Table 2. v2 adds results for other editors and models, batch/sequential reversal, KL divergence and downstream capabilities. For example, new Table 6 reports 99.45% tracing accuracy for MEND/GPT2-XL and 1.89% for AlphaEdit/GPT2-XL. These expand the reported findings rather than establish gains on the original experiments.

T1.justification: v1 Section 6 explicitly grants access to the original model, including the pre-edit matrix. v2 Section 2 revises the formal access assumption to exclude that matrix and defines tracing and reversal using post-edit parameters. The SVD construction and other mathematical derivations remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is supplied.

C1.justification: v1 frames its contributions around detecting, tracing and reversing ROME edits. v2 broadens the central claims to tracing and reversal across several editing methods, explicitly without the original edited weights, and adds recovery of the original output distribution as a claimed outcome. The original weight-pattern and relation-prediction contributions remain in the appendices.

C2.justification: v2 distinguishes removing an edit from recovering the original behavior and discusses capability preservation. It adds explanations linking AlphaEdit's poor tracing performance and larger reversal thresholds to reduced overfitting and null-space projection. v1's single-edit limitation is replaced by experiments and discussion of model-dependent batch/sequential robustness and failures.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project repository link, online-editing and hypernetwork-source information, and matrix dimensions for additional models. However, v1 Appendix D.1's A100-80GB hardware disclosure and GPU-day breakdown disappear. Core tracing hyperparameters and dataset-construction details remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for r-ROME, AlphaEdit, additional models and downstream benchmarks, and broadens the ROME-specific positioning. Its relationship to earlier prompt-dependent edit detection and in-context reversal remains substantially the same. Publication updates to already cited works do not constitute new related work.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion are substantially rewritten around two principal tasks. A new Problem Statement replaces the main-text background, while ROME background, weight-pattern analysis and relation prediction move to Appendices B–D. The tracing method receives the name EditScope, and the appendix structure is extensively reorganized.

P2.justification: The overview diagram is revised, CounterFact and Yago tracing plots are combined in Figure 3, and diagnostic displays move to the appendices. Table 2 gains Qwen columns, several retained tables lose uncertainty columns, and new KL, capability and multi-edit displays are added. These are substantial display and layout changes beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's single-editor, single-edit setting. Distribution-recovery and downstream-capability checks, seeded tracing evaluation, and multi-editor/batch/sequential experiments address important gaps while exposing AlphaEdit tracing failures. Some older uncertainty and compute disclosures are lost, and capability checks cover only ROME on Llama3. Nevertheless, the new evidence materially improves understanding of both effectiveness and applicability.
